walkthroughs.body_html:
Networks — a core area of GCSE Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Networks brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Networks.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: One advantage of a peer-to-peer network is that it:
options: Needs no expensive dedicated server, so it is cheap and simple for small setups
Gives the best security for large companies
Centralises all backups automatically
Eliminates the need for any cables or Wi-Fi
The maximum rate at which data can be transferred over a connection
The physical width of the network cable
The number of users on a network
The size of the computer screen

mcqs.q: Is bandwidth the distance a signal can travel?
options: No - bandwidth is the capacity of a connection in bits per second; how far a signal reaches is range, a separate property.
Yes - bandwidth is measured in metres.
Yes - higher bandwidth means the Wi-Fi reaches further.
Yes - LAN stands for Line-Attached Network.

mcqs.q: In a client-server network, are the clients just dumb screens with no processing power?
options: Yes - bandwidth is measured in metres.
Yes - only the server does any computing in a client-server network.
Yes - clients are keyboards connected directly to the server.
No - clients are full computers that run their own software; they simply request central services such as file storage, email or printing from servers.
Yes - clients are keyboards connected directly to the server.
No - a LAN is defined by its small geographic area, not its medium; wireless LANs (Wi-Fi) are still LANs.
Yes - LAN stands for Line-Attached Network.
Yes - wireless networks are never classed as LANs.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “LAN”?
options: A wide area network connecting devices or whole LANs over large geographical distances, usually over leased or public infrastructure.
A device that forwards data packets between different networks, choosing a suitable route towards each packet's destination address.
The maximum rate at which data can be transferred over a connection, usually measured in bits per second.
A local area network covering a small area such as a home, school or office, with the infrastructure owned by the organisation itself.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “WAN”?
options: A local area network covering a small area such as a home, school or office, with the infrastructure owned by the organisation itself.
A wide area network connecting devices or whole LANs over large geographical distances, usually over leased or public infrastructure.
The maximum rate at which data can be transferred over a connection, usually measured in bits per second.
A network in which all devices have equal status, sharing resources directly with each other without a dedicated central server.
